column2: Being Best Man: A Year of admin, Stag Dos and One Panic-Free Speech
社交生活
被任命为伴郎的一年:单身派对、请柬回执、致辞写作与婚礼当天,一份关于友谊与项目管理的田野笔记。
B2

The message arrived at midnight and contained the four most dangerous words in male friendship: "You're my best man." My oldest friend was getting married, and I had just been handed a year-long project with no salary, no training and one unmissable deadline. I said yes with the confidence of a man who had never organised anything more complex than a picnic, then lay awake composing a mental risk register that grew longer with every item. A year later, standing in a borrowed suit with a speech in my pocket and both groom and rings accounted for, I finally understood: being best man is simply project management wearing a bow tie, held together by checklists and by asking for help earlier than pride suggests.

The stag do was the first deliverable, and I over-engineered it like a rookie. Ten men, two nights, one coastal city, and a spreadsheet with colour-coded contingencies. What I learned instead, over one chaotic and joyful weekend, was that the plan's job is not to control events but to guarantee the essentials: beds booked, one shared meal per day, a sober navigator, and a hard rule that nobody's phone dies. I had built the weekend around the groom's actual tastes — a boat trip, a curry, a football match, zero fancy dress, because he hates fancy dress — and that single act of listening earned me more credit than any activity would have. The hangover was monumental. The reputation, somehow, was excellent.

The paperwork phase taught me about the quiet machinery of weddings. There were RSVPs to chase (my unofficial role, since the couple were drowning), a group gift to coordinate without letting it become a ledger of grudges, and the seating plan, which I now regard as the hardest logic puzzle sold as a social nicety. The plus-one question demanded diplomacy: two guests were mid-breakup with each other, an uncle's opinions were considered a hazard by the bride's mother, and somebody had to sit near the door with an escape route. I learned to phone instead of text for anything emotional, to confirm everything twice, and to keep a single master list, because information scattered across four chat threads is information lost.

The speech was the deliverable I feared most, and the way through it surprised me. I tried to be funny first, and the drafts were terrible — jokes about the groom that landed only if you already loved him. The turn came when I accepted the actual job of the speech: it is not a roast, it is a handover. I was retiring as the person who had held the "chief companion" contract and formally welcoming my successor. I wrote one page: how we met, one story with a lesson, what I had watched him become, and a welcome to her that treated her as the accomplished adult she is rather than a mysterious acquisition. Rehearsals happened in the car. The only jokes I kept were the ones where the groom's dignity survived, and the maid of honour and I compared notes beforehand so our speeches didn't rhyme.

The wedding day itself ran on delegation. My kit — the rings, the speech, a spare handkerchief, paracetamol, safety pins, a phone charger, and the schedule printed on a card the size of a passport — stayed in one inner pocket and became known, by the end of the day, as "the ministry". My duties were mostly invisible: driving the groom when his hands were shaking, telling the photographer where the couple actually were, standing in the right photographs, and saying, at intervals, the sentence that holds any wedding together: "Everything is fine, and if it isn't, nobody needs to know yet." The caterer's van got lost; the guests never heard about it. That, I learned, is the whole job.

Looking back from the honeymoon photos (not mine), the year left me with a philosophy I now apply to everything: a celebration is a project, a project is a list, and a list is a form of love. The spreadsheet saved the stag do; the phone calls saved the seating plan; the page-long speech saved me from myself. But the parts people still talk about were never on any list — the toast where the groom's father cried, the dance-off nobody planned, the bride's shouted amendment to my speech ("he forgot to mention I organise him now!"). Plan the skeleton, protect the essentials, and let the muscle do what it likes. That is how you survive being best man, and possibly how you survive most things.
